title: The Names of the Word
english: … at once in these words the mystery, deep and great, which needs to be taught from above. For it was revealed in this way to the divine Peter (compare Matthew 16:16–17). For the Word was and is God, equal in glory with God the Father and sharing His throne, existing with Him and coeternal with Him. His names before the incarnation, those that are in some way proper to His nature, are God, Wisdom, Light, Life and Power, and besides these, others that are found in the sacred Scriptures.

But since He lowered Himself into self-emptying, being made in the likeness of man and found in form as a man (Philippians 2:7), He receives the common name, that is, Christ and Jesus, or else “God with us”; for “with us” means being in our condition. For it is written: “Behold, the virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel” (Matthew 1:23; Isaiah 7:14). And the blessed Gabriel, revealing the mystery to the holy virgin, the Mother of God, says: “Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God. And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you will call his name Jesus” (Luke 1:30–31). “For he will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21).

Have the blessed angel and the prophet, then, spoken words that cannot be reconciled with each other? Not at all. For the divine prophet, speaking mysteries in the Spirit, announced beforehand God made to be with us, giving Him this name from His nature and from His dispensation in the flesh. The blessed angel, for his part, gave Him the name from what He does; for He has saved His own people. That is why He has been called Savior. Indeed, when He underwent birth according to the flesh for our sake, the hosts of angels brought the shepherds the good news of the birth, saying: “Do not be afraid; for behold, we bring you good news today of a great joy, which is for all the people: today a Savior has been born, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David” (Luke 2:10–11).

So He is Emmanuel because, being God by nature, He came to be with us, that is, became man; and Jesus because, being God and having become man, He was to save the world under heaven. When, then, He came forth from His own mother’s womb (for He was born of her according to the flesh), then His name was also called (Isaiah 49:1). So I say that the name Christ does not suit God the Word before His birth according to the flesh. For if He had not yet been anointed, how could He be called Christ? When He came forth as man from His mother’s womb, then He receives the name, together with His birth according to the flesh.

He says that His mouth was made like a sharp sword (Isaiah 49:2). This too is true. For it is written somewhere about Him, or rather the prophet Isaiah himself says: “And He shall be girded about the waist with righteousness, and wrapped in truth about the …” (Isaiah 11:5).
translator_notes: The section begins and ends mid-sentence (…λεν ἐν τούτοις / εἰλημμένος τὰς); both breaks are marked with an ellipsis.
ἰσοκλεής is 'equal in glory', ὁμόθρονος 'sharing the throne'; ἦν καὶ ἔστι 'was and is'.
The Emmanuel quotation has καλέσουσι, the form of Matthew 1:23 (Isaiah 7:14 LXX has καλέσεις). Gabriel's words join Luke 1:30–31 to Matthew 1:21.
ἐκ τῆς ἐνεργείας: the angel names Christ from His saving work, not from the angel's own activity.
Lemmas in view: Isaiah 49:1–2 (called from the womb; mouth like a sharp sword). The closing quotation is Isaiah 11:5 LXX.

title: The Acceptable Time and the Prayer in Gethsemane
english: … like us, and entered the measure of self-emptying. He addresses the chosen and says: “In an acceptable time I have listened to you, and on a day of salvation I have helped you” (Isaiah 49:8). Christ and His mystery were foreknown before the foundation of the world (1 Peter 1:20), but they shone forth at the times the Sovereign willed, the times at which He has helped us; and the time of the incarnation he calls a day of salvation. So too, somewhere, the divine Paul says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2). And the prophet David sings and says: “This is the day that the Lord has made; let us exult and be glad in it” (Psalm 118:24).

“And I have given you as a covenant to the nations, to establish the earth and to inherit the inheritance of the desert, saying to those in bonds, ‘Come out,’ and to those in darkness, ‘Show yourselves.’ And in all their ways they will be fed, and in all the paths will be their pasture. They will not hunger or thirst, nor will the burning heat or the sun strike them; but He who has mercy on them will comfort them, and will lead them by springs of water. And I will make every mountain a road, and every path a pasture for them. Behold, these come from afar, these from the north, and these from the sea, and others from the land of the Persians” (Isaiah 49:8–12).

Some of the earlier interpreters decided to make the beginning of the present chapter the words: “Thus says the Lord: In an acceptable time I have listened to you, and on a day of salvation I have helped you” (Isaiah 49:8). And they say that these words were spoken by God the Father to Christ, the Savior of us all. They weave in besides a meaning of this kind. He prayed, they say, before the precious cross, saying: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39); and He was not heard, for He drank it. But since He trampled on death with the Father’s help, the words “In an acceptable time I have listened to you, and on a day of salvation I have helped you” were of necessity said to Him.

But this account seems to me to be sorely lacking in plausibility. For He knew that He had to drink the cup, and that the world under heaven could not come to be saved except through the death of His flesh and the resurrection from the dead. Even so, He went through the form of the prayer as a carefully chosen step in the divine plan, so that His begging to be spared the Passion might accuse the bloodguilt of the Jews. For how would Israel have become liable to the charges of impiety against Him, if suffering had not been against His will because of its shame? Yet even so it became His will, both to take away sin from the world and to remake our state into the newness of a holy life (compare Romans 6:4). For in this way one will understand also His saying: “I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will …” (John 6:38).
translator_notes: The section begins and ends mid-word (καθ' ἡμᾶς … τὸ θέλημ); both breaks are marked with an ellipsis.

The view that Isaiah 49:8 is spoken by the Father to Christ after an unheard Gethsemane prayer belongs to 'some of the earlier interpreters'; Cyril reports it and rejects it (δοκεῖ … πολὺ τὸ εὐπίθανον ἀῤῥωστεῖν ὁ λόγος).
πέπωκε γὰρ αὐτό: 'for He drank it'. ἀντιλαμβανομένου τοῦ Πατρός: 'with the Father's help'.
Psalm 117:24 LXX is Psalm 118:24 in English numbering. The lemma is Isaiah 49:8–12 LXX (ἐκ γῆς Περσῶν).

title: The Church's Growth Through Faith
english: … shows the multitude of those who will be called, how great and countless it will be. “For your sons,” he says, “whom you have lost, will say in your ears: Make room for me” (Isaiah 49:20). It is said somewhere to the spiritual Zion as well: “Enlarge the place of your tent and of your curtains; fix them firm. Do not hold back; spread out still further to the right and to the left” (Isaiah 54:2–3). We have read also in the books of Moses that around the tabernacle in the wilderness, the one made, I mean, of skins, wide and long courts were laid out, some facing the dawn and the sunrise, some to the west behind the tabernacle, and to the north and the south as well (compare Exodus 27:9–18). The figure hinted at the breadth and length that the sacred courts, that is, the churches, would have in time to come.

Yet even so, since the grace from Christ keeps on overflowing, the places everywhere are too narrow for those who have believed, so that the Church, which is the spiritual Zion, in her joy reflects and cries out within herself: “Who has begotten these for me?” (Isaiah 49:21). And I would say: faith in Christ. For through it you, who were childless and a widow, have become great in children. It has reared your peoples for you; and you who were once left alone have grown rich beyond all expectation, and have been seen with many children, you who were once bare and alone.

“Thus says the Lord: Behold, I lift up my hand to the nations, and to the islands I will raise up my signal, and they will bring your sons in their bosom, and carry your daughters on their shoulders. And kings will be your foster fathers, and princesses your nurses, on the face of the earth; and they will bow down to you and lick the dust of your feet. And you will know that I am the Lord, and you will not be ashamed or put to confusion” (Isaiah 49:22–23).

He has promised Zion that she will have many children, and fine ones, and that her children will come to such a multitude that she will need wider places than before and will be urged to enlarge her tent. Now he at once shows that the multitude of the children promised to her appears not so much from Israel as from the flock of the nations. And the thing is true, and one can see it from the events themselves. For the remnant of those from Israel has been saved, but it is small and easily counted (compare Romans 11:5); while the world under heaven has been caught in the net through faith in Christ, and the power of the apostolic and gospel preaching has brought to Him those throughout all the earth.

That this will happen, then, he makes plain by saying: “Behold, I lift up my hand to the nations” (Isaiah 49:22). “Lift up” means “raise high” and “exalt”; and the hand would suggest strength, that is, power. For when Christ was made known to the nations through the gospel preaching, He became exalted and renowned through the miracles He worked, and through the resurrection …
